query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: Controlled DSC experiments performed under an inert atmosphere, when analyzed using the lever‐rule and integrated with CALPHAD modeling, will yield accurate estimates for the melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties for chemically homogeneous, single‐phase high-entropy alloys with errors within roughly 5–10% of independent measurement techniques.
generation.material_initial_state: Homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloy samples (e.g., equiatomic or near-equiatomic solid-solution alloys) prepared by methods such as arc melting or additive manufacturing.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to controlled heating experiments using DSC (and, optionally, complementary dilatometry or in situ structural imaging) under inert conditions and integrate the resulting thermal data with CALPHAD predictions to extract the key thermodynamic parameters.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted at ambient pressure under an inert atmosphere using standardized, controlled heating rates spanning from below the solidus up to above the melting point, ensuring minimal kinetic effects and supercooling.
generation.structural_mediator: The configurational entropy that stabilizes the single-phase solid solution and underpins the distinct thermal signatures observed at the onset of melting.
generation.mechanism: As the material is heated, DSC traces are expected to reveal a characteristic jump in specific heat near the melting transition; application of the lever rule to thermal expansion or DSC curves allows phase fraction deconvolution. This thermal response, when correlated with CALPHAD-predicted thermodynamic data, enables extraction of melting temperature, latent heat (fusion enthalpy), entropy change, and volume change across the transition.
generation.predicted_outcome: For high-entropy alloys that are single-phase, the measured melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy and volume change will align with CALPHAD predictions within an approximate accuracy range of 5–10%, indicative of both the method’s efficiency and reliability.
generation.baseline: Similar DSC-based methods combined with CALPHAD modeling have proven effective in simpler metallic systems, and previous HEA studies using lever rule analysis have yielded comparable performance.
generation.boundary: This approach is expected to be valid primarily for HEAs with a confirmed single-phase, homogeneous structure; its accuracy may be compromised in alloys exhibiting significant multiphase behavior or inhomogeneities.
generation.uncertainty: In systems with incipient secondary phase formation or local compositional variations, the deconvolution of overlapping thermal signals may introduce uncertainties exceeding the 10% threshold.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of high-entropy alloy samples confirmed by structural analysis (e.g., XRD, microscopy) to be single-phase. Conduct DSC experiments under inert atmospheric conditions with controlled heating rates spanning below the solidus to above the liquidus. Complement these measurements with independent dilatometry (or in situ neutron imaging) to determine volume changes and latent heat. Use CALPHAD modeling to predict the thermodynamic parameters. Compare the DSC/CALPHAD-derived values with those from the independent techniques over multiple alloy compositions.
measurements: DSC thermograms and derived specific heat curves
Calculated latent heat (fusion enthalpy) and fusion entropy via integration and lever rule analysis
Volume change at melting via dilatometry or in situ imaging
CALPHAD model predictions of melting temperature and thermodynamic parameters
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, for the majority of the tested single-phase HEA samples, the DSC + CALPHAD approach yields melting temperatures, fusion enthalpies/entropies, or volume changes that consistently deviate by more than approximately 10% from those obtained via independent measurement techniques, then the proposed method would be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: An integrated multiscale simulation approach, which combines high-throughput CALPHAD predictions with enhanced molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, can accurately and efficiently determine the melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the high-entropy-alloy family.
drafts.material_initial_state: Homogeneous high-entropy alloys synthesized with uniform mixing of four or more principal elements.
drafts.intervention: Apply a dual simulation protocol: (1) Use existing CALPHAD databases tailored for multi-component systems to obtain a baseline of thermodynamic parameters; (2) Integrate these results with atomic-scale MD simulations employing enhanced sampling techniques to capture local disorder and configurational effects.
drafts.conditions: Computations performed across the full melting regime; validated by experiments such as differential scanning calorimetry and high-temperature dilatometry under controlled ambient or inert atmospheres.
drafts.structural_mediator: Atomic-scale structural disorder and local chemical variations that influence melting behavior and liquid-phase properties.
drafts.mechanism: CALPHAD methods provide an efficient baseline using bulk thermodynamic data, while MD simulations account for local atomic interactions and disorder—especially significant in HEAs—that collectively determine the precise melting kinetics and phase transitions. This multiscale approach bridges the gap between macroscopic thermodynamic models and microscopic atomic behavior.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The integrated model is expected to predict melting temperatures within approximately ±50 K of experimental values, with fusion enthalpy and entropy within ±5% error, and volume changes at melting within ±3% error, along with a reliable estimation of liquid-phase properties such as density and viscosity.
drafts.baseline: Traditional single-scale approaches (e.g., CALPHAD-only or MD-only) typically show larger errors and are less efficient when applied to HEAs, due primarily to their inability to capture the full effects of chemical complexity and local structural disorder.
drafts.boundary: The method is applicable to high-entropy alloys consisting of four or more principal elements with relatively random mixing; its performance may degrade in systems exhibiting significant short-range order, phase segregation, or in cases where CALPHAD database coverage for certain elements is limited.

Then, experimentally measure these properties using differential scanning calorimetry, high-temperature dilatometry, and liquid-phase property probes (e.g., viscosity and density measurements) under consistent conditions.

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the majority of alloy samples (e.g., at least 4 out of 5 tested compositions) show prediction errors exceeding approximately ±50 K for melting temperature, ±5% for fusion enthalpy/entropy, or ±3% for volume change, then the integrated approach would be considered falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Advanced atomistic simulations—integrating phase coexistence techniques with enhanced sampling (e.g., metadynamics) applied to molecular dynamics—can accurately determine melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with errors below 5% relative to precise experimental measurements.
drafts.material_initial_state: A crystalline high-entropy alloy (HEA) sample with multiple principal elements uniformly distributed.
drafts.intervention: Run molecular dynamics simulations that combine a phase coexistence setup with metadynamics or similar enhanced sampling methods to accelerate the occurrence of melting and solidification events.
drafts.conditions: Simulations performed under controlled pressure and temperature conditions that span a range below and above the expected melting point. The approach is applied across various HEA compositions (typically 5 or more elements) and for systems where disorder and potential elemental segregation are moderate.
drafts.structural_mediator: The evolving interface between the solid and liquid phases, which mediates energy exchange and allows direct measurement of latent heat and volume changes associated with the melting transition.
drafts.mechanism: The phase coexistence method provides a dynamic equilibrium between phases that, when combined with enhanced sampling, overcomes high activation barriers typical in HEAs. This enables the accurate extraction of thermodynamic quantities, as the fluctuations at the interface yield statistical measures of enthalpy, entropy, and volume differences between phases.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The simulation approach predicts melting temperatures, latent heats (enthalpy of fusion), fusion entropies, changes in volume at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic behavior that agree within approximately 5% of values obtained from high-precision experiments.
drafts.baseline: Baseline data are state-of-the-art experimental measurements and high-fidelity thermodynamic assessments of specific HEA compositions.
drafts.boundary: The method is expected to be most reliable for HEAs with moderate compositional complexity and low to moderate segregation. In cases where extreme chemical ordering or significant local compositional fluctuations occur, discrepancies may exceed the 5% error margin.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a set of HEA compositions with well-documented experimental melting parameters. Perform molecular dynamics simulations as outlined (combining phase coexistence with enhanced sampling) for each composition. Compare the derived values for melting temperature, enthalpy of fusion, fusion entropy, and volume change with experimental data. Repeat the simulations with different interatomic potentials to assess robustness.

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the simulation-derived properties differ by more than 5% from experimental measurements across multiple HEA compositions or if the method fails to converge consistently, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: A combined high‐throughput experimental–computational approach that integrates differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), high‐temperature dilatometry, and in situ neutron imaging with CALPHAD‐based modeling can accurately and efficiently determine the melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties for single‐phase high-entropy alloys.
drafts.material_initial_state: As-cast, chemically homogeneous high-entropy alloys that have been confirmed to be single-phase solid solutions.
drafts.intervention: Subject the alloys to controlled heating in an inert atmosphere while performing simultaneous DSC measurements to record heat capacity changes, high-temperature dilatometry to capture volume changes, and in situ neutron imaging to monitor liquid-state mixing and phase evolution. Then, integrate these measurements with CALPHAD predictions and low-temperature Debye T3-law-based extrapolations.
drafts.conditions: Experiments conducted over a temperature range from well below the solidus (to apply Debye extrapolation for cp) up to the fully melted state, under an inert (or vacuum) atmosphere to prevent oxidation. A standardized heating rate is used to minimize kinetic effects.
drafts.structural_mediator: The configurational entropy that stabilizes the single-phase structure, along with minimal secondary phase formation, ensures that the measured thermal signals (cp jump, latent heat release, and volume jump) can be directly related to the fusion properties.
drafts.mechanism: The rapid increase in cp near the solidus followed by an abrupt endothermic peak in DSC is used to extract the enthalpy of fusion. Integrating the cp curve (after accounting for the Debye T3-law behavior at lower temperatures) yields the entropy of fusion. In parallel, dilatometry provides the volume change at melting while in situ neutron imaging can confirm the continuity (or remixing) of the liquid phase, serving as a structural cross-check. CALPHAD modeling then provides a thermodynamic framework to relate all these data for accurate predictions.
drafts.predicted_outcome: For HEAs that are single-phase in the solid state, one would expect to consistently measure melting temperatures, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, and volume changes that agree with CALPHAD predictions within an error margin of approximately 5–10%. This integrated approach should also reveal predictable trends as a function of alloy composition.
drafts.baseline: Traditional DSC or dilatometry measurements performed individually without simultaneous structural (neutron imaging) validation or integration with CALPHAD modeling, which typically yield less reliable or less efficient determination of the full liquid-phase thermodynamic properties.
drafts.boundary: This approach is expected to be valid for high-entropy alloys that form single-phase solid solutions and exhibit clear, non-overlapping melting features. In alloys with significant multiphase behavior or strong short-range ordering effects, the interpretation may be complicated.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a set of single-phase high-entropy alloys spanning a defined compositional space. Perform synchronized high-temperature DSC, dilatometry, and in situ neutron imaging experiments under identical heating conditions. Independently calculate fusion properties by integrating cps (using Debye T3-law extrapolation at lower temperatures) and measure volume changes. Compare these experimental values with CALPHAD-model predicted values.
measurements: DSC heat flow and derived cp curves
Integrated latent heat (fusion enthalpy) and derived fusion entropy
Volume change at melting from dilatometry
Liquid state phase evolution from neutron imaging
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, across multiple HEA samples, the experimentally derived melting temperatures, fusion enthalpies or entropies, or volume changes differ systematically from the CALPHAD-model predictions by more than about 20% (taking into account experimental uncertainties) or if the liquid-state imaging reveals phase inhomogeneities inconsistent with the single-phase assumption, then the proposed integrated approach is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) measurements combined with lever‐rule analyses and CALPHAD-based modeling can be used to accurately and efficiently determine the melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid‐phase thermodynamic properties of high-entropy alloys. This integrated approach exploits the fact that the configurational entropy stabilizing the single-phase solid solution also defines sharp thermodynamic signatures at melting that are detectable via changes in specific heat.
drafts.material_initial_state: Homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloy samples (e.g., equiatomic or near-equiatomic solid-solution alloys) prepared via methods such as arc melting or additive manufacturing.
drafts.intervention: Subject samples to controlled DSC experiments under inert atmosphere from room temperature up to and beyond the solidus/melting onset; apply lever rule analysis on the thermal expansion or DSC curves to separate phase contributions; complement these measurements with CALPHAD modeling to extract enthalpic and entropic contributions.
drafts.conditions: Ambient pressure under inert atmosphere with carefully controlled heating rates to avoid supercooling; applicable in temperature regimes spanning from well below the melting point to above the liquidus.
drafts.structural_mediator: The configurational entropy (and its interplay with enthalpic penalties) that governs phase stability and transitions in high-entropy alloys serves as the mediator linking thermal signatures to microscopic melting behavior.
drafts.mechanism: DSC traces reveal the sudden increase in specific heat at the onset of melting while the lever rule can deconvolute coexisting phases; combining these observations with CALPHAD predictions allows the extraction of melting-point depression effects, fusion enthalpy/entropy values, and volume changes. This rationale is founded on the established relationships from the Gibbs free energy (G = H - TS) framework, where the robust entropy term in HEAs is key.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Measured melting temperatures, fusion enthalpy and entropy, and volume change at melting will agree with CALPHAD predictions within an approximate accuracy range of 5–10% when applied to single-phase HEAs, demonstrating the approach's efficiency and reliability across a broad compositional space.
drafts.baseline: Similar DSC and CALPHAD approaches have successfully determined thermodynamic properties in simpler metallic systems and some HEA studies (e.g., using lever rule analysis in thermal expansion data) show comparable performance.
drafts.boundary: The approach is expected to work best for HEAs that form a well-defined, single-phase solid solution; for alloys with significant secondary phases or inhomogeneities, the extraction of precise thermodynamic parameters may be compromised.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of high-entropy alloy samples covering a range of compositions (including well-established single-phase and multi-phase systems). Conduct DSC measurements with controlled heating rates complemented by structural analysis (e.g., XRD, microscopy) to verify phase homogeneity. Independently determine fusion enthalpy/entropy and volume change using a separate method (e.g., high-temperature dilatometry or neutron imaging) and compare to values predicted using the DSC + CALPHAD approach.
measurements: DSC thermograms showing specific heat capacity changes at melting
Thermal expansion curves for lever rule-based phase fraction analysis
XRD for phase identification and verification of single-phase nature
Dilatometry or neutron imaging to independently measure melting volume changes
CALPHAD model predictions of thermodynamic parameters
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the DSC + CALPHAD approach yields thermodynamic parameters (melting temperature, ΔHfusion, ΔSfusion, and volume change) that deviate by more than ~10% from the independently measured values or if the method consistently fails in single-phase HEAs where the model assumptions hold, then the proposed approach would be falsified.
